name: Adam Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the clarinet section in a civic wind band, record short advert stings, the brief musical openings to adverts, and teach six pupils at a music centre. I earned a music master’s and younger players ask me to show difficult passages, but my pay is typical for this trade. I like the moment a section settles into one pitch.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What has to fit around those rehearsals?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner manages a school office, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. We have about four months of expenses saved. There are some nearby bands, but their paid seats open only when someone leaves, and school pickup still sets our evening limit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that a faster rehearsal email is useful if the fee is written beside the date. A clarinet still has to tune to the player next to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our four-month reserve and my partner’s school-office wage make a delayed advert fee manageable. A whole cancelled concert would matter, but this mild AI picture does not make me expect one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep paid band rehearsals and six music-centre pupils this season. I sometimes use AI to sort booking messages, then check every call against the band’s signed sheet; before next season I would ask for a written concert cancellation fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about the household under this small change. The mortgage is covered by work already on our calendars.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did the last cancelled concert cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A storm moved one outdoor concert and we lost half the fee. I would ask for that half in writing before another outdoor season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you tell a pupil who plays too loudly?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I tell them to hear the other clarinet first. A loud right note can still be the wrong answer in a band.

say: I would welcome **faster rehearsal emails** with fees written beside dates.
I would seek a **written half-fee term** for cancelled concerts.
think: Our **four-month reserve** and partner pay handle one delayed advert fee.
A **cancelled concert** would still hurt, though AI does not cause it here.
do: Keep **paid band rehearsals** and six music-centre pupils this season.
Request a **written half-fee cancellation term** before the next outdoor season.
feel: I feel **calm** because current bookings and household pay cover the mortgage.
S0.quote: A loud right note can still be the wrong answer in a band.
fieldNote: His **senior skill** brings typical musician pay with a four-month reserve and steady second income.
Occasional **AI booking help** is checked against the signed band sheet.

steps.text: Keep paid civic band rehearsals and six music-centre pupils this season
Request written half-fee cancellation term before next outdoor concert season

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band manager that software may write cheap advert stings and move rehearsals faster. I would ask clients for written fees on every revision before recording again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stings provide about a quarter of my own pay, and I could lose some buyers. Live band work should continue, though a shorter season would make the four-month reserve feel small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I would ask the band librarian for a paid hour showing me a new AI score-alignment tool, which marks where recorded notes should meet the printed part. In the first year I would test it only on a clarinet part and recording I own without pupil names, compare every mark by playing the paper score, and stop if it shifts a note or sends the file outside the band library; I would not buy a trial subscription.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about a real cut to my own recording pay. I can learn a proved tool, but the client still has to buy a player.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the librarian has no paid time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my paper part and wait for a paid demonstration. Learning a tool on an unpaid evening would take time from pupils and family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you put a pupil recording into it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I would use only a track I own without a child’s name. If the library cannot explain where the file goes, the test stops.

say: I would seek **written revision fees** before recording again.
I would tell the manager that **live players** still need paid calls.
think: Advert stings provide **one quarter** of my own earnings.
A shorter **band season** could shrink income despite the reserve.
do: Request **written revision fees** and a paid librarian demonstration before new recording work.
Test **score alignment** only on nameless owned files; play paper changes and stop on wrong notes or library leakage.
Refuse a **paid trial subscription** and wait if training is unpaid.
feel: I feel **anxious** about possible lost stings and shorter live work.
S1.quote: Learning a tool on an unpaid evening would take time from pupils and family.
fieldNote: His **new AI learning** needs paid instruction, a nameless owned part, manual playing and a library privacy stop.
He keeps **revision fees** written rather than offering free work to preserve clients.

steps.text: Test score aligner after paid librarian demo on owned nameless files; play changes, stop on errors/leakage
Keep paid band and pupils while refusing unpaid tool training or subscription
Request written revision fees before recording again

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that thinking AGI by 2028 could make advert stings cheaply. Playing robots follow around 2031, three years later, so we must sign live dates rather than count on them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the advert clients to stop ordering my stings in 2028, removing a quarter of my pay. Paid band rehearsals may also fall, but that is not certain, and our four months saved leave some search time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I would count sting invoices and ask for the signed band season. In the first year after 2028, if stings stop and paid band rehearsals fall, I would apply for a posted school clarinet-tutor role only if my master’s and any required licence qualify, written net pay after travel and childcare beats lost fees and pickup fits; I would keep band and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious about expected advert loss, though we have some savings and nearby bands. I would be alarmed if live rehearsals also vanished, but I cannot say they will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you book a teaching course now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would read a real school post before paying for any licence. My present degree may already meet the requirements.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you compare a new timetable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would use the written hours and net wage after travel and childcare. A friend’s guess about a school job would not replace a paid rehearsal.

say: I would distinguish **2028 thinking AGI** from 2031 playing robots.
I would seek a **signed band season** before judging other seats.
think: I expect **sting orders** to end in 2028, removing a quarter of my own music pay.
Paid **band cuts** remain possible but uncertain while the current season still has signed rehearsals.
do: Count **sting invoices** and request the signed band season this week.
Seek **posted tutor work** only if 2028 stings and rehearsals fall, qualified, written net pay beats losses and pickup fits.
Keep **band and pupils** until a suitable written school offer is signed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about expected recording loss with savings and local options.
S2.quote: A friend’s guess about a school job would not replace a paid rehearsal.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 advert loss** precedes 2031 playing robots and removes a quarter of his pay.
A school move requires **posted eligibility**, written net replacement pay after travel/childcare, pickup and signed offer.

steps.text: Seek eligible posted tutor role if 2028 stings and rehearsals fall; replacement written net-after-travel/childcare, pickup
Keep paid band and six pupils until suitable written school offer is signed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the band that five years until AGI by 2031 lets us build a paid place to teach reed care, looking after the thin strip that vibrates in a clarinet mouthpiece. Playing robots follow around 2034, after advert writing changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stings may end in 2031, but a separate reed clinic could replace some of that money. I would need families to pay for my preparation and supplies, not just promise to attend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I would ask a separate community hall for an available Saturday room after the children’s pickup. I would run a four-week reed clinic only if seven families prepay enough to cover hall hire, reed supplies, my teaching and preparation, and the hall checks loan clarinets or pupils bring sound instruments; in the first year after 2031 I would renew it only if seven still prepay those costs, the room remains available after pickup and instruments stay safe. I would keep my current pupils and band dates while paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be anxious until the clinic earns after supplies and my time. Five years before AGI lets me test a paid reed clinic without spending our mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which instrument would you refuse?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would refuse a loan clarinet with a cracked mouthpiece or loose key. If the hall cannot inspect its loans, families must bring safe instruments or I cancel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if only four families prepay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four fees would not cover the reeds, hall and my preparation. I would refund them and keep my six regular pupils.

say: I would offer a **paid reed clinic** with real prepayments.
I would refund a **four-family group** that cannot cover costs.
think: Advert **sting fees** could end by 2031 before 2034 robots.
Seven **prepaid families** must cover supplies, hall and my work.
do: Start **reed clinic** only with seven prepayments covering hall, supplies, teaching/preparation, pickup fit and inspected loan or sound own instruments.
Renew **paid clinic** after 2031 only if seven prepay hall, reeds and teaching/preparation, room remains available after pickup and instruments stay safe.
Keep **paid band dates** and six pupils while booked.
feel: I feel **anxious** until the independent clinic covers my time and supplies.
S3.quote: Five years before AGI lets me test a paid reed clinic without spending our mortgage reserve.
fieldNote: The **separate clinic** needs seven prepayments for hall, supplies and paid teaching/preparation.
Loan clarinets need **inspection** or pupils bring sound instruments, with child pickup covered.

steps.text: Start clinic if seven prepay hall/supplies/teaching/prep, room fits pickup, loans inspected or instruments safe
Renew clinic after 2031 if seven prepay hall/reeds/teaching/prep, room available after pickup and instruments safe
Keep paid band rehearsals and six pupils while booked
Refund four prepayments rather than teach without covered reeds, hall and preparation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my children that ten years until AGI by 2036 is time to build a craft and ask what it pays. Robots able to play a clarinet come around 2039, after software changes the advert trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 53 I may still lead the clarinet section, but the mortgage arrives every month until then. Four months saved and some nearby bands let us plan without pretending every future concert is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would save a quarter of each extra paid advert-sting fee after food and mortgage until our reserve reaches six months. Across the decade I would run the separate reed clinic only with seven prepayments covering hall, reeds, teaching and preparation, safe instruments and a room after pickup; in the first year after 2036 I would seek a posted school ensemble post only if paid band dates fall, the school accepts my qualifications, written net pay after travel and childcare replaces lost fees and pickup fits. I would keep band and pupils until a written offer is signed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel uneasy about the distant concert contract while this season remains paid. A long warning lets us grow savings from real fees, not an unsigned advert.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if advert orders stop before six months?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would save spare paid pupil fees after bills and keep three months untouched. A client’s warm words are not money in the account.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take a school title for less money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need posted hours and a written net wage that covers the lost band dates and pickup. I would keep playing until a signed school offer exists.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the advert stings could stop before I know whether the band pays for next season. Signed band dates, a posted eligible school role with written net pay and workable pickup, and a paid reed clinic would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who checks the mouthpiece before a child borrows a clarinet. A good lesson cannot begin on an instrument that hurts to play.

headlineQuote: A good lesson cannot begin on an instrument that hurts to play.
portrait: At **43**, Adam leads civic-band clarinets with a music master’s and strong skill, records advert stings and teaches six pupils.
His **typical musician pay**, school-office partner, mortgage, two children and four-month reserve make delayed dates noticeable.
He uses **AI occasionally** for booking and learns score alignment only after paid instruction with owned files and manual playing.
He tests a **paid reed clinic** only with seven prepayments covering supplies, hall and teaching, safe clarinets and pickup.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could end advert stings before the band confirms next season’s paid dates.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed band dates**, a posted eligible school role with viable written net pay and pickup, and a prepaid clinic would help.
